turns.prompt_text: what would a recursive function for permutation with repeats look like
turns.response_html:
To generate permutations with repeats (also known as $n$-tuples), a recursive function iterates through every possible element at each position. Since elements can be reused, you do not need to track which items have already been selected.

Python Implementation

def permutations_with_repeats(elements, length, current_permutation=[]):
    # Base case: if the current permutation has reached the desired length
    if len(current_permutation) == length:
        print(current_permutation)
        return

    # Recursive step: try every element for the current position
    for item in elements:
        permutations_with_repeats(elements, length, current_permutation + [item])

Key Concepts

  • Recursion Depth: The function calls itself until the current_permutation matches the target length.
  • Branching Factor: For a set of size $n$, the function branches $n$ times at every level.
  • Total Permutations: The number of results is calculated as $n^r$, where $n$ is the number of elements and $r$ is the length.

turns.prompt_text: what's the mathematical form of this
turns.response_html:
The mathematical form of permutations with repeats is an ordered $k$-tuple (or $r$-tuple) drawn from a set of $n$ elements.

The Formula

For a set of size $n$, the number of possible permutations of length $r$ is:

$$P^R(n, r) = n^r$$

Definition

Given a set $S$ where $|S| = n$, a permutation with repeats is any element of the Cartesian product:

$$S^r = \underbrace{S \times S \times \dots \times S}_{r \text{ times}}$$

Step-by-Step Logic

  1. Selection: You have $n$ choices for the first position.
  2. Repetition: Because elements can be reused, you still have $n$ choices for the second position, the third, and so on.
  3. Product Rule: By the fundamental counting principle, you multiply the choices for each of the $r$ positions: $$n \cdot n \cdot n \dots (r \text{ times}) = n^r$$

turns.prompt_text: what about just for permutation what would the recursive mathematical function look like
turns.response_html:
The recursive mathematical form for a permutation of $n$ elements taken $r$ at a time, denoted as $P(n, r)$, can be defined by the following recurrence relation:

$$P(n, r) = n \cdot P(n-1, r-1)$$

Formal Definition

For the base cases and constraints:

  • Base Case: $P(n, 0) = 1$ (There is only one way to arrange zero elements).
  • Recursive Step: $P(n, r) = n \cdot (n-1) \cdot (n-2) \dots (n-r+1)$.

This represents selecting one element from $n$ options and then finding the permutations for the remaining $r-1$ positions from the $n-1$ remaining elements.

The number of combinations with repetition (also known as multichoose) is the number of ways to select $r$ items from a set of $n$ where order doesn't matter and items can be reused.

The Formula

This is often called the Stars and Bars formula:

$$\binom{n+r-1}{r} = \frac{(n+r-1)!}{r!(n-1)!}$$

Recursive Definition

The recursive form, $C^R(n, r)$, follows the logic that for any item, you either include it at least once or you don't include it at all:

$$C^R(n, r) = C^R(n, r-1) + C^R(n-1, r)$$

  • $C^R(n, r-1)$: You chose the current item, so you still have $n$ items to choose from for the remaining $r-1$ slots.
  • $C^R(n-1, r)$: You decided not to use the current item at all, so you must choose all $r$ items from the remaining $n-1$ options.

Base Cases:

  • $C^R(n, 0) = 1$
  • $C^R(1, r) = 1$

In combinatorics, a combination refers to selecting $r$ items from a set of $n$ where the order does not matter.

The Formula

The standard formula (also known as the binomial coefficient) is:

$$\binom{n}{r} = \frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}$$

Recursive Mathematical Form (Pascal's Identity)

The recursive definition is based on the logic that for a specific item, you either include it or exclude it:

$$\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n-1}{r-1} + \binom{n-1}{r}$$

  • $\binom{n-1}{r-1}$: You pick a specific item, so you must choose $r-1$ more from the remaining $n-1$.
  • $\binom{n-1}{r}$: You skip that item, so you must still choose $r$ items from the remaining $n-1$.

Base Cases:

  • $\binom{n}{0} = 1$
  • $\binom{n}{n} = 1$
  • $\binom{n}{r} = 0$ if $r > n$
